youtube.title: Who discovered penicillin? A holiday and a dirty dish 🧫
youtube.description:
The factories, the chemists, or the third one? A doctor came back from holiday, picked up a dish he had left out, and saw a mould killing the bacteria around it. Then nothing happened for more than a decade: nobody could make enough. The first patient improved, and the supply ran out. Three men shared a Nobel Prize; a fourth was left out.
Which did you pick?

research.topic: Discovery of penicillin: on 3 September 1928 Alexander Fleming, bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital, London, returning from holiday, noticed a Penicillium mould on a staphylococcus culture plate with a clear zone where the bacteria had been killed; he published in 1929 (British Journal of Experimental Pathology) but could not purify or stabilise the substance. In 1939–40 Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, Norman Heatley and colleagues at the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, Oxford, produced usable penicillin and showed in May 1940 that it protected mice (Lancet, August 1940). The first patient, Oxford policeman Albert Alexander, was treated on 12 February 1941 and improved markedly, but the supply ran out and he died in March 1941. Large-scale production was developed in the United States (Peoria USDA laboratory, Pfizer, Merck and others) from 1941; penicillin became available to the US public in March 1945. Germany's leading antibacterials of the time were the sulfonamides (Prontosil, Gerhard Domagk, 1935). The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1945 was shared equally by Fleming, Chain and Florey; Heatley received no prize.

myths.myth: Penicillin was an American wartime invention.
myths.reality: The United States industrialised production from 1941 onward, but the mould was observed at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1928 and first turned into a working drug at Oxford in 1940.

myths.myth: Fleming discovered it, made it, and cured people with it.
myths.reality: Fleming observed and named it but could not purify it; the Oxford team of Florey, Chain and Heatley made it usable twelve years later, and the first patient was treated in 1941.

landscape.our_gap: Penicillin clips retell the Fleming anecdote as a talking head; nobody raises the real wartime production photo out of the country on a map, splits FOUND 1928 from MADE 1940, and names the man the Nobel left out as a quiz.
